faq.a: An estimate of how well your kidneys filter blood, calculated from a blood test; lower numbers mean less function.
Lost function usually cannot be restored, but progression can be slowed substantially with treatment.

name: Kidney Protection and Diabetic Kidney Disease
blurb: Chronic kidney disease, albuminuria, eGFR and kidney outcome trials.
title: Kidney Protection and Diabetic Kidney Disease
answer: Diabetes is the leading cause of kidney failure. SGLT2 inhibitors slow kidney decline, and the FLOW trial showed semaglutide reduced major kidney outcomes by about 24 percent in people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, with lower deaths from any cause.

sections.body: Ask for a yearly urine albumin test and eGFR; catching kidney disease early lets protective drugs do the most good.
sections.heading: What it means for patients

explainer:
Kidney damage in diabetes shows up first as albumin, a protein, leaking into the urine, measured as the urine albumin to creatinine ratio, and later as a falling estimated glomerular filtration rate, eGFR, a measure of filtering capacity. Both are cheap tests, and guidelines recommend them at least yearly.

SGLT2 inhibitors reduce pressure inside the kidney's filters and slow decline, independent of their glucose effect. GLP-1 drugs appear to protect through several routes, including lower blood pressure, weight loss, reduced inflammation and effects on blood vessels. Blood pressure control and drugs that block the renin angiotensin system remain foundations, and newer drugs such as finerenone add further protection for some people.

developments.text: The FLOW trial found semaglutide reduced the risk of major kidney disease events by 24 percent and all cause death by about 20 percent in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease.
FLOW subgroup analyses found the kidney and survival benefits were consistent across cardiovascular risk groups.
A 52-week randomised trial in Nature Medicine studied how semaglutide protects the kidney, finding effects not explained by glucose lowering alone.
A prespecified pooled analysis of the SELECT, FLOW and SOUL trials examined semaglutide's effect on kidney outcomes across people with and without diabetes.
